utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As the witness in coming in, we can make arrangements for the closed session continuation of the hearing. No, just bring him in. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Phillips.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination will continue. I simply have to remind you that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the outset of your evidence continues to apply until it finishes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. 15 [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So your cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman will now continue. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going to start this morning in tab 4, page 4991, and your comment there is from "I don't know" and I think maybe it's just some random notes you made on the 14th of December. It doesn't indicate that you were meeting with anyone in particular.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What line are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at 4991, there's only one line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I assume that should read: "Demaqi's number one goal is Rugova. He hates him and wants to destroy Rugova before -- he will destroy any meeting he is in and any meeting he is not in." Now when you say he will destroy any meeting he's in and any meeting he's not in are you referring to Demaqi or Rugova or someone else making that reference?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was just a random note I made to myself based on one meeting with Demaqi and Demaqi is referring to Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who is the "he" you're -- the "he" is Demaqi referring to Rugova?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "he" equals Demaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Demaqi will destroy any meeting he's in or Demaqi is saying Rugova will destroy any meeting he's in?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Demaqi hates him and wants to destroy Rugova and any meeting that he's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I understand now. Thank you. If you go over to the next page there's a little more about that, about halfway down, and this is a summary page I think you've written regarding the day of 15 December 1998. You say about halfway down, a paragraph that brings with: "The Holbrooke press conference." "Holbrooke really wants this thing to get going" -- I assume "this thing" is some kind of a settlement conference. "Holbrooke really wants this thing to get doing but Demaqi seems to be the sticking point. He wants to bring Rugova down. He hates him. Destroying Rugova is his number one goal." Am I correct that what Holbrooke is talking about there is the settlement conference of some kind?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, could counsel remind us the reference to the passage he just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go on over now to page 4995, this is a note being made rather late at night, it looks like 11.40 at night p.m. You put at the top: "Headline: Relationship off the skids, don't know why." And then you make the comment: "Too aggressive, my fault." I can't figure out what it is you're talking about there. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could help you. I don't recall either. I usually made many notes to myself at night about things, and I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go to tab 5 now, the first page, 6661. The head refers to a KVCC visit. I don't know what KVCC is. Can you tell us or not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boy, I just don't recall. Kosovo Verification Committee Council or something like that. I believe this was in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's some reasonable --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's coordination group or -- it's a group that we worked with in Vienna, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And just a little ways down there's a reference to SacEur. Was that General Clark?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what he means when he says: "He's the tip of the spear?" Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The reference here to General Clark, who is somebody for whom we are seeking admission so I know that -- well, admission of his evidence so I know that it is to some degree relevant to the case. However, the question may tend to invite the witness to get into areas that he would not be qualified to speak about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think he's only being asked what he recorded as having been said by General Clark. I understand your difficulty with this, Mr. Stamp, because this is all outwith the examination. Everything that's happened this morning is beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's within the realms of what was conceded yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be you envisage something closer to the examination-in-chief taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, I asked for restraint. I understand there is material counsel might well -- it might well be unfair if counsel cannot cross-examine from the disclosed material. However, to ask if General Clark said, that is one thing; to ask about what General Clark means and what was operating on General Clark's mind at the time goes beyond what the witness can speak of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless it's something that he -- you know because of the context knows and can clarify, because it isn't very -- it's one of these statements that would need some further interpretation probably. So let's find out if he's got a clear recollection and invite him not to speculate. Would that be satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know for sure what this was a reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or would you be speculating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I can speak to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a general military term that most commanders use. When they say they're the tip of the spear it means that they're the leader, the decision-maker, they're the ones who will call the decision for what's needed. So it's a general term. All military commanders can use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help with the situation this morning, Colonel, by advising you. If I ask a question that you have any discomfort, please let us know and if it's a question that would require you to speculate, please let us know because, I don't want you to speculate about any -- I only want you to talk about things you can give us some information on if you're reasonably certain about. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never tell you I could speak about something if I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't noticed your hesitation in that regard before. Let's go forward to 6686 and make some progress here. It refers to a meeting at 4.45 on 21 December, that is that you call a tank meeting. Can you tell us what a tank meeting is.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Apparently General Clark was at whatever kind of a meeting this was.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you not there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just cannot comment on it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to push it. I'm going to respect your wish in that regard. If we go to page 6689, 21 December 1998, apparently it's the end of the week and you're making some notes about the week and you say this: "What a week. We bombed Iraq for four days, Clinton was impeached by the house, and Kosovo is coming apart, and Clark just told us the NATO extraction force is not going to be there for us." Now, those are your notes just kind of summing up what you call an interesting week.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I do have about that is that event of Iraq being bombed for four days, that was a -- that was an event that got significant media coverage, not just in the US but all over Europe and in the Balkans and everywhere, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any television available to me. I think I saw a newspaper article or two on the bombing, but it was more speak within the OSCE office of what had gone on and the internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There might be another occasion when you and Mr. Phillips can have a general chat about events that he recorded affecting the world in general, Mr. Ackerman, but it would be helpful if you could concentrate on the issues in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a point there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There usually is when I intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the argument from that point is that the bombing in Iraq was a precursor that people in Kosovo could see on their television sets and understand if NATO started bombing, it was going to look like that and they ought to get out of there. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears to me, although it's not extremely clear from your notes, that you and General Walker went off to Washington over the end-of-year/beginning of 1999 period and that you were in Washington for several meetings. Am I correct on that assumption?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we went home for new year's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And while you were in Washington you had a number of meetings. Let's go to page 6639, and this is on 30 December of 1998 and it's a meeting that takes place at the state department. And one of the things that apparently was important enough for you to make a note about was the state department was anxious that the OSCE-KVM mission produce a bi-monthly noncompliance and noncooperation marker reporting.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In other words, they wanted better reporting on noncompliance with the cease-fire, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just say that they just wanted reporting, not necessarily a better report or a -- let's call it report -- just wanted reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did bi-monthly mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wanted it twice a month, every couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not every two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, it should say actually bi -- yeah, it was twice a month they were looking for a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go back to page 6636, you had a meeting on the 30th of December at 10.00 in the morning apparently with (redacted)and (redacted). Now, is it true that (redacted)was the chairman of the joint chiefs at that point?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not the chairman of the joint chiefs at that point. He never was the chairman of the joint chiefs. He was the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, the (redacted). Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page, 6636?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 6. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And (redacted) would have would have been an (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an (redacted), I believe, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at the next page, (redacted) seems to be the speaker. "If the UCK overplays its hand, a complete collapse of the cease-fire occurs and we will have to pull the Kosovo Verification Mission out." Was the US in a position to make that decision to pull the verification mission out?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That again is going into the government policy -- government capacity, so the witness cannot comment on it. I mean, he might have an opinion, but it is not really within his bailiwick of work or experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Stamp, and this is also a territory about political considerations of a rather complex situation that's not really advancing our knowledge of the events that really matter in the case, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, there's a significant point to make based on this rather innocuous-looking phrase. Let me try a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it was the case that -- if the UCK overplayed its hand, causing a KVM pull-out, a KVM pull-out would really mean a beginning of NATO bombing, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that's within the capacity of the witness to answer. We have had the top people -- or the top man from NATO here already to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the issue I'm trying to get at, and maybe I'm not being very clear about it, if the KLA at any level understood that by overplaying their hands they could bring on NATO bombing it basically put KLA in control of whether NATO would bomb or not. That's the point I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's argumentive and not a matter for this witness to make a judgement on. So please proceed to something he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree it's argumentive, but I think I need to lay some kind of a basis for making that argument. That's all I'm trying to do. And I'm going to move on because you've asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right underneath that particular phrase Walker speaks about the verification mission and what is going on there. And he says: "We're doing more than we were chartered to do. We're doing more than watching and reporting." That's what he said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's in my notes. Yes, sir, I'm certain that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go over to page 6646, it's the 6th of January, I think you were still in Washington and Walker is conducting an interview with Doyle McMannis of the LA Times and based on your responses yesterday, you probably don't remember Doyle McMannis of the LA Times. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember Doyle McMannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do remember --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm from Los Angeles, so I connected too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 6646 apparently there's a question from McMannis: "What does this have to do with verification?" And Walker apparently responds this way: "It is necessary as part of our security," but then he says this: "I don't think Milosevic wants the mission to fail, but he does not want it to succeed either." And was that your understanding based on your knowledge there of Milosevic's view, that he really didn't want the mission to fail?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly have no idea what Mr. Milosevic was thinking. This was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to even consider that question, Mr. Phillips.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm only interested in that if you were in a meeting with Milosevic where he made the statement that he didn't want the mission to fail. I don't want you to speculate. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you never heard Milosevic say that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that statement from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Page 6650, we're at 6 January, and you're meeting with (redacted), and this may be another area of some sensitivity. If you look at the bottom of page 6650, it appears that your note seems to indicate that (redacted) made the following or a similar statement. "Bosnia may have been simpler because we really had victims. Here it's more complicated. The KLA are bad people, drug-trafficking and so forth. There are hard-line KLA. They have, however, achieved some popular support." I take it you were present in that meeting and made that note based upon what you heard?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to go to 6652 and again I'm guessing a little bit. It looks like what's going on in those notes is that Ambassador Walker is interviewing with the Voice of America.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. He apparently told the Voice of America that US senators, plural, and then among them apparently Dick Lugar want US policy in FRY to change to remove Milosevic. Is that what General Walker told Voice of America at that point?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker made that comment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that wasn't the first time you had heard interest in certain circles about the necessity of removing Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard it before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And removing Milosevic was not something that was going to happen as a result of negotiations, was it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You think there was any way to forge an agreement with Milosevic to abdicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, this is really not for the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that question. Let's move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we move on, sometimes when a passage is cited, it might well be proper to cite the whole sentence instead of a phrase in a sentence. Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got the chance to re-examine him on that, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But it also puts the question in context for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless it's some --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- blatant misrepresentation then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it is not. I wouldn't accuse anybody of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to tab 7, page 6588 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, when you started this, I had the impression it was some focused exercise that you were going to embark upon and that is why you prepared the bundle of papers, but it sounds as though it's a sort of general trot through the diary or notebook without much particular focus except to demonstrate just what a complex political situation this was, which doesn't help us to determine whether excessive force was used, which is really the issue with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think there are more issues than that with this witness, by just looking at his diary. He was present at a lot of very important meetings and has a lot of very important information about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what four American senators thought should happen to Milosevic is neither here nor there as far as we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may have something to do with why for reasons that I think are still open to discussion NATO might have precipitously attacked to get rid of Milosevic when they realised it couldn't be done politically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the events that led to that much more closely related to that than the views of American senators that might have been held by many people around the world. But these are not the men in power at the time who have the ultimate decision. We're more concerned with the people who were actually controlling the work of NATO rather than people who had opinions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think American senators and congressmen, Your Honour, tend to have great influence with American presidents, at that time Bill Clinton, who had great influence with Wesley Clark and NATO, who made the decision to attack Yugoslavia. So I think it's extremely relevant if what their goal was at that time was to get rid of Milosevic. The theory of the Prosecution in this case and the theory we keep hearing from the opening statement on is that this was some kind of a humanitarian mission because of an escalation of attacks upon the Albanian people, and what I want to argue and what I'm suggesting with this line of cross-examination is that that wasn't the mission at all. The mission was to get rid of Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how much longer do you envisage being on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This particular subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, your cross-examination in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It looks like 10 or 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue, but try to identify more significant events than the views of American senators, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 7, page 6615. And this is notes you made at 2.10 in the afternoon. I don't know who all of the players are, but I take it that the W that you refer there is Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And on 15 January 1999 you recorded Walker as saying: "Our request is the same, to remove Milosevic"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment to read through the note there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, please do.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I can -- I can speak to your question if there is one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question is: That's what Walker said on that occasion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can tell us. I'd appreciate it if you can, but if you can't please say so. Who was the president that's referred to in your notes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djukanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he was from Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. 6652, I think we're over to tab 9 now -- actually, I want to go to -- 6652 is actually in tab 6. We're back at that Voice of America interview and a person named Maja Drucker apparently asks Walker: "Is your KVM's mission, mission impossible?" And Walker says: "Some things have gotten better since KVM has been in place." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was true, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if we go to page 6654, 6 January 1999, there was something called a Kosovo round-table. And unless you're comfortable with it, you don't have to tell us what that was, but there's a note there about access to VJ sites. And it says: "Getting better with one-hour notification." So apparently things were improving in that regard also; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specifics, but I do know that we had been working very hard with our VJ LO and the Serb side to get access to those sites. They were requiring one-hour notification; we were trying to meet that. We had less obstacles at that point. I don't know how many sites that we got to actually verify, though, in that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 6590, it's now 9 January and there's a conference call --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What tab was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're in tab 7, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is following another event where some MUP were ambushed and where the KLA took a bunch of VJ soldiers as prisoners, kidnapped them. There's a suggestion here by Walker on page 6590 that I just don't understand, and if you can explain it, I'd appreciate it. "Walker cautions that want to be careful that we don't play into Milosevic's hands and have him emerge as the great humanitarian and crisis solver. We want to keep all this away from Milosevic." Do you have any idea what that's about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would just be speculation at this point. I can't give you a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Who's the person named Kai Eide, K-a-i E-i-d-e?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Norwegian Ambassador on the council, OSCE in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if you can deal with this without a little more context. If you look at page 4934 in tab 8 I can tell you that the subject matter here deals with the Racak incident and the reactions to that incident. And your note indicates that General Walker was disappointed with a statement out of Vienna where Kai Eide says: "We're overstating our situation here in Kosovo, PC suggests we lighten up." Are you familiar with that event?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that did have to do with the reaction to Racak, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell me what PC is, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Permanent council, OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to 27 January now, we're at page 6549 at tab 9. And we're getting late into the month of January. There's a meeting apparently with Walker (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can't comment on the conjecture of what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. 6569, this is a meeting that I think Walker had with a person described as political director, Dr. Gunter Pleuger. Can you tell us who that was.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently, according to your note, Walker, in discussing the role of KVM, said: "We are having an effect on the ground wherever we are."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were there, you know that that's true, and you also, I think, know that the KVM contingent had not yet built itself up to full strength, it was still short a number of people from getting the number of verifiers thought necessary. I think at that point you had, according to Walker on this page, about 1150 and your goal was 2.000, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And your observations were that when you were able to be there in these various areas that you were having an effect on what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we were having an effect on keeping a cease-fire intact, which was our main goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So ramping that mission on up to its strength of 2.000 or perhaps beyond in Walker's view, and I take it also in your view, would have had a further salient effect on what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my last question is tab 10, 4906, along the same line. We're now all the way over into mid-February. I think you and Walker have gone to Russia, to Moscow?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're meeting with Lieutenant-General Nikolai Zlenko in the ministry of defence?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Walker tells him with regard to the mission: "We're up and running and making a sizeable difference in Kosovo;" correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement is consistent with, quite frankly, many meetings that we had with the Contact Group countries and it was often said to keep it in a positive light because we needed the verifiers and we needed the support of the Contact Group. So we were very optimistic whenever we went out about the contact nations to give a positive view of what OSCE was doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But as you told me a moment ago you, in fact, were accomplishing things when you were able to have people on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Colonel, my name is Dan Ivetic and I'm going to have some questions for you today. I represent Mr. Lukic. It's important for you to pay close attention to my questions, and likewise even though we both want to try and finish the examination as soon as possible, since we both speak the same language we need to be careful not to speak over one another and to have a pause between our words for the sake of the translators. Okay, sir, so the first thing I would like to ask you about is your testimony yesterday, it's the bottom of page 9 and the top of page 10 of the transcript, wherein you testified that Mr. Lukic, whose first name you previously stated you did not know, was introduced to you as "the personal representative of Milosevic." First of all, do you recall who made that representation to you and when?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would have been early November 1998 in our first meetings at the government building with Mr. Sainovic as we were meeting all of the Serb representatives for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you previously testified at page 7, lines 18 through 19, that Mr. Lukic presented himself as the chief of the MUP from Pristina. So let me try and clear this up. In your 2001 interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, you identify Mr. Loncar as being presented as a "personal representative of Milosevic," but in that interview, in fact, Mr. Lukic is not identified in that capacity and, indeed to the contrary, you repeat that he was merely introduced as the chief of the MUP. Now, Mr. Loncar testified here that he indeed was brought out of retirement by Milosevic. Is it possible that you are mixing your recollections of Mr. Loncar and Mr. Lukic, since now for the first time yesterday you mentioned Mr. Lukic as being a personal representative of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we turn to your notebook later on we will again see that Mr. Lukic is not referred as a personal representative of Milosevic, but the question I have for you is if we can move to -- strike that. I think you had already answered yesterday that the notes that are contained in your notebook are taken contemporaneous with the events that you eye-witnessed or took part in on the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notes weren't taken, you know, at the moment; usually when I got back or even the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Much closer to the actual events than your testimony, say, yesterday or today?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can now move to your role in the KVM. Can you tell me precisely what written agreements were in existence which you know of and had access to that guided the work of the KVM mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me -- you want to know if I read the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the agreement in Warsaw, I think, the initial -- the initial OSCE agreement mandate that we were to execute in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you read any of the corollary agreements, such as the Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement, the --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall all of the documents that were in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, If we can focus for a moment on the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement, which is e-court exhibit P658 and the paragraph I want is on page 2 of the same. And I don't know whether you need to have that up on the screen, sir. My question is fairly specific, so I will proceed and we'll see if you can answer it without referring to the document. Part 1 in paragraph 9 of the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement specifies that the FRY government and its entities will designate former liaison officers to work with the KVM in Belgrade, Pristina, and field locations. The question I have for you, sir, is with respect to this provision of the agreement: Do you know who the formal liaison officer for the whole Serbian MUP was that was supposed to liaise with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the Serb member was from the MUP, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the name now. Then I was familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we need to be in closed session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would say no, but I am going to be referring to his 2001 interview and to his notes at least once, and I don't know if we want to just keep -- it might be easier just to have the whole thing in closed. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it a lengthy cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will remain where we are in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I should be done in about 20 minutes, Your Honour, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I told you that the MUP liaison officer with the KVM at all times was a Colonel Miroslav Mijatovic, would that extemporise you or does that sound --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you ever had any dealings with Colonel Mijatovic of the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I met him maybe once or twice through our own liaison officer when we went to their headquarters to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, in your 2001 interview with the Office of the Prosecutor that took place in Washington, DC, specifically on the third page of that interview, you have described Mr. Lukic, as among other things, as being short. Now, my client is just between 1 metre 85 and 1 metre 90 centimetres. Is this what you meant by short or is there a possibility that the individual that you are describing is not Mr. Lukic but is some other officer from the MUP that was present for these first meetings?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that Mr. Lukic was in the meetings with Mr. Sainovic in the government building, was introduced as such to me. I don't recall his height at this point or even that note, but if it's in my notes obviously I said it. But I knew who Mr. Lukic was in our meetings with Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall -- do you recall how tall Colonel Mijatovic was? Was he taller or shorter than General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have heard testimony from other KVM personnel that in fact Colonel Mijatovic and not General Lukic was involved in the regular contact and meetings with the KVM. Is it possible that you are talking about Colonel Mijatovic when you describe the General Lukic in your interview as being short?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can speak to you, counsel, is the -- General Lukic was in our meetings with Sainovic. I don't recall his size. I know Mr. Mijatovic was the individual that our KVM team met with on a weekly basis. I never met with him during those liaison discussions; it was our own MUP-KVM liaison officer that did those meetings. We often got reports back from him on the results of those meetings when we had questions about excessive MUP activities or force being applied to a village. He was accessible to us and cooperative with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well, we'll -- before we go to the meetings I'd like to just ask a couple questions about something you testified about yesterday at page 4 lines 18 through 22 about the town of Malisevo. And yesterday you stated that you didn't understand why the MUP was in Malisevo because there was no reason for them to be there. The question I have for you is: Do you know that the MUP was required by their agreement with the US-KDOM to remove their stationary forces from certain villages and was specifically directed to station them all in Malisevo, the so-called Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that there was some police to be required in some of those villages. Malisevo was a village that we wanted to make an example to show what would happen if we removed some of the threat some of the Albanian population would repopulate those villages. So that was our push to show the success you could have by removing what was considered a provocative force in one of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But my question for you, sir, and -- I apologise, I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. My question for you, sir, is when you made your statement yesterday that you don't know why the MUP was in Malisevo there was no reason for them to be there, were you aware of the fact that indeed, the Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement told them to be in Malisevo at part 3, on page 1?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the KDOM piece. The notes there were my notes -- myself thinking out loud and I often did that in my notes. My comment to myself there was no one there to protect and so hence my note about don't know why they're there. There's nothing there to protect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now we can move to the meetings. And again, I apologise, I'm waiting for them to watch up to us. We'll get done with this quickly, no problems there. Now, what I want to ask you is relative to the meetings you attended where Serbian MUP personnel were present, am I correct that you always memorialised these and took notes in your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say always. Sometimes, you know, we were in a listening mode to an issue or a concern, and I may have participated in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. All the meetings with the top leadership ought to be memorialised in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A good number of them are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday when you testified that Mr. Lukic was present for all such meetings except for the one on the day of Racak. Now, if we --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not exactly correct. I said Mr. Sainovic, I believe -- I have to check my own transcript, but I thought that I said that Mr. Sainovic was not available and we called for a meeting and all we could meet with was Mr. Loncar as a result of the Racak event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'm focusing on Mr. Lukic now not Mr. Loncar. I believe you testified that Mr. Lukic was present for all the meetings except for that one with Mr. Loncar on the 15th of January, 1999. Now --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic was not present for some of the early meetings when we first set up the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies things quite a bit for me because I was just about to ask you about that time-period. Indeed if we look at your notebooks, I can't find Mr. Lukic as being present for any of the various meetings in November of 1998. The first reference to him comes up in the December 24th, 1998, meeting, and I want to ask you about that. If we can pull up your notes. I did not make a nice book with tabs because my reference to the notes was going to be very limited. So this will have to be on the screen, sir, it's Exhibit P2835 at page 36. And hopefully this will be the page of your notes dealing with the 24 December 1998 meeting at 1815 hours. That's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The next page, I believe, Your Honour. That's interesting, my printed copy has different page numbers than the one in e-court, so I apologise, sir. If we turn to the next page which will be 37 in e-court, we hopefully have this meeting that I am going to ask you some questions about. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we take a look at this entry first of all. We see General Lukic is identified as being one of the attendees for the hearing. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I have on my notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall that Mr. Lukic was specially requested to be present at that meeting at the behest of Mr. Walker due to the incident that occurred involving with Mr. Walker and a purported assailant with a alleged grenade?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a grenade, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mr. Lukic was present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reason he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And indeed this is the -- what is described in your notes as the second meeting with Sainovic, that is at page 3 of your notes where it says Lukic was introduced at this meeting as the commander or the chief of the MUP. So does that refresh your recollection as to whether perhaps this is the first meeting where Mr. Lukic was present?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That makes sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, great. Now, if we can turn to -- I have in my notes page 38, so I assume it's going to be page 39 of the e-court version. I want to focus in on precisely what Mr. Lukic said at this meeting because the -- your notes record that he only said two or perhaps three lines. And the amount to talking about the investigation to this incident with Walker saying: "All persons talked to," and then there's interruption and it looks like the translator finishes what Mr. Lukic said by saying: "Say never saw the grenade. "We consider the results of the investigation as having no grenade." If this is all that you wrote down for Mr. Lukic from this meeting, can we conclude this is all of significance that Mr. Lukic said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would conclude that. The majority of the meeting was fairly hotly contested issue between Mr. Walker and Mr. Sainovic, more by Mr. Walker. He was upset about this event and that it hadn't been investigated properly, and he was demanding Mr. Lukic do more and was speaking to Mr. Sainovic to allow that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But as far as Mr. Lukic is concerned, if --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Said very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, instead of going through your notebook page by page, I'd like to short-circuit this a bit and I think I'm being fair. I have gone through the entire set of the notebooks that we have, which means essentially from November through February 16th, 1999, since I guess the one notebook after February is missing. In those notebooks there is a total of just one meeting wherein Sreten Lukic is noted as having attended, and that, in fact, is this meeting of the 24th of December, 1998, that we've just gone through. Can we, therefore, sir, conclude that your observations about Mr. Lukic are based solely on this one encounter where he stated two or three lines of discussion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't draw that conclusion. I was inconsistent with -- in several of my meetings of putting down who each of the players were at the meeting on both sides, both the OSCE side and whether it be the KLA side or the Serb side. But I'm confident that Mr. Lukic was present at more than that one meeting when we met Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But if your notes don't have any reference to Mr. Lukic, then you cannot be certain what meetings, apart from this one, he was present at?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific on the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, I'd like to focus back on the issue of MUP liaisons. Do you know whether -- I presume that the KVM had a liaison officer for contacts with the MUP. I think you talked about him previously. Do you know who this individual at the KVM was that was tasked with being the MUP liaison?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Lieutenant-Colonel Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with an individual by the name after Guy Sands?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with Guy Sands, too. We had -- we had a different liaisons, we had a few. Guy Sands, I think, was also involved -- no, Ciaglinski was the VJ I believe,. Guy Sands was the MUP and then we had one more who was also a British individual who was a liaison officer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that you yourself personally did not have an exact picture of the functioning of the structure of the police forces in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, perfect. Now, I have just a few more questions about specific areas of your testimony. Now, first of all, would you agree with me that the KDOM was doing the work of KVM during the time period when your mission was still being set up?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes..

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in fact according to the KVM agreement it's at P658 page 1, section number 5 if it needs to be up on the screen, but I submit it's explicitly stated in that provision that KDOM will act in place of the OSCE verification mission pending its establishment and once the OSCE operation KDOM will be absorbed by the verification mission. Now, was it your understanding and do you recall that KDOM had a duty to apprise the KVM mission, once it was set up, of all the efforts that had been undertaken by KDOM on its behalf in the nascent stage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you talked about the fact that the Serbs did not give you any information relative to mines. If I can focus on that just for a moment. On the MUP side are you aware of the fact that Vlastimir Djordjevic issued a written report to the American embassy in Belgrade, which would have been the seat of the US-KDOM on the 30th of October, 1998, specifying that although the MUP did not utilise any mines in its activities, it had come across and defused or destroyed mines in various villages and was aware of incidents where Red Cross vehicles and vehicles of others KDOMs had run across mines and was providing a list to the KDOM all such villages where mines were known to exist, either from incidents or from the MUP uncovering them and defusing them. Are you aware of that fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to get to the original question, am I aware of the fact that the Serbs provided my information to KDOM?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In October of 1998, before the KVM was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was not aware of that. I was aware that we had asked specifically for that same information from the Serbian authorities, from a KVM perspective. Did not ask KDOM for that, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now another issue the base-line figures for forces. As far as the MUP is concerned, are you aware of the fact that also in October of 1998, the KDOM -- the US-KDOM fully negotiated a base-line with the MUP and that a report was issued to KDOM establishing that base-line of being just over 10.000 individuals, a reduction of about 4.000 and some-odd personnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the KDOM. I am aware of the request that KVM asked for and never received, base-line information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the last question for you. General Maisonneuve the KVM chief in Prizren testified that he in fact was aware of this base-line figure negotiated on the part of the KDOM. How do you explain the fact that the KVM leadership didn't know but the persons out in the field did know about this KDOM information and indeed used it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can only --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That -- I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I think the objection would have been well-founded. What the question should have been said is: Can you explain it? And then we could find out --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain that. I know Ambassador Walker never received what he asked for, whether his deputies in the field missions had that data, they never provided it to our ops chief which was General DZ. I could not explain why they wouldn't have provided that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I guess I do have one more question. I'm waiting for the transcript. Do you know whether Ambassador Wal er or in fact anyone at the KVM leadership asked Shaun Byrnes were KDOM for this information, since there was an obligation on the part of KDOM to provide information?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Ambassador Walker expressed his concern of not having that information in front of those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, Colonel. I'm completed with my cross-examination of you. I thank you for your time and your patience.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Re-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Closed or open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we should continue in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- or perhaps I could just ask the one closed session matter and then we could move into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown an extract from your notebooks, tab 7, page 6615.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 6615. And you were read a passage in which Mr. Walker is recorded as saying: "Our request is the same, to remove Milosevic." In what context was he speaking? Who was he speaking to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is speaking to President Djukanovic in Montenegro, and the context of that remark was Ambassador Walker felt that we were not receiving a level of cooperation from the Serb authorities that he would have liked. He felt that Milosevic was that obstacle and it was difficult for KVM to have full and unfettered access in Kosovo with Milosevic calling the plays. He felt that he was responsible for many of the -- of the difficulties in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And by "our request," do you know what that means when he's saying that to Mr. Djukanovic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We may go into open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to take you through some of your evidence and ask you to clarify something. You said when I asked you questions first that you met -- or you were present at a meeting where Mr. Milutinovic was present with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many meetings were you present at that Mr. Milutinovic was present at?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- I'm going to object to this. In direct examination my friend asked the witness whether he recalled a meeting on the 15th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want the witness to be here while you're making this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Maybe it's best that he leave, yes. I think it should be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you just leave the courtroom briefly, please, Mr. Phillips, while we deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my submission is this, that my learned friend on direct examination asked the witness if he recalled a meeting with Mr. Milosevic on the 15th of December, 1998. He answered that it was on the 24th of November, 1998. He explored that meeting with the witness, and at no time during direct did he ask the witness whether there was any other meeting. He asked only about that one encounter on the 24th. It was open to the Prosecution to ask whether there were other meetings at which he was present, the witness was present with Mr. Milosevic. That should have been done on direct. It's not appropriate to open this question on re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless he was only concerned about one issue and therefore essentially about one meeting and the matter is now in a different state from when he was examining the witness and clarification is sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, my point is he could have explored that with the witness on direct examination and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but he may have taken the view it was pointless in view of the answers he got. He was satisfied with the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You then had a very successful cross-examination, and the -- in view of the very first question Mr. Stamp asked in examination-in-chief, it may be that it's an issue over which there is some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- I mean, I understand the point you're making. I have no difficulty understanding your point, but I think this often happens with cross-examination and what the Prosecutor may have thought was a simple issue is clearly not as simple as he regarded it at the time. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that may require clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any other point you want to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, except I may -- depending on where it goes, I may seek leave to re-cross, but I'll do that if it arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your response to this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the evidence of the witness was pretty clear in examination-in-chief, but when he was cross-examined he was cross-examined on point about a date, the 24th of November, and he indicated in cross-examination or appeared to indicate that he was not sure about the date. So there might not have been a meeting with Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Milosevic on that date, the 24th of November, and he did indicate that there were at least two meetings in which Mr. Milutinovic was present involving two letters, one letter being a letter explaining the context of the KVM mission and one letter being a letter of complaint and that the letter explaining the context -- the meeting in respect to the letter explaining the context of the KVM mission was a friendly meeting, and I think that was brought out by one of the Defence counsel in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When do you say that the witness claimed there were at least two meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think the witness explicitly said there were at least two meetings. The witness spoke about meetings, one in respect to a letter dealing with the framework of the KVM mission and he said that was a friendly meeting. He spoke of another meeting dealing with complaints that Mr. Walker transmitted in another letter. And he says that was a meeting in which Mr. Milosevic was shouting. So it appears from what -- from what came out in cross-examination - and it's not necessarily the cross-examination of Mr. O'Sullivan - that the witness is uncertain as to the date and he's uncertain as to whether or not the -- the letter that he spoke of in examination-in-chief was the letter or was the letter that afforded the occasion for the meeting he described in examination-in-chief. Yes, it's being pointed out to me now at page 11945 of the transcript, and I'm not sure who is asking questions here. The witness says -- or the witness is asked: "You say it went out on Wednesday 25th of November, that is a letter, and what I'm wondering is whether you actually discussed this letter with Mr. Milosevic on the 24th when you say it didn't go out on the next day, the 25th." The witness answered: "Yeah, all good points, I'm clearly confused with the dates. We met with Milosevic. We delivered a letter to him that made him upset. You know, I would have to go back and look at the dates, but even now I'm confused now on what the date is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's immaterial. The question in relation to whatever date it was is whether Mr. Milutinovic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the passage goes on: "Q. Now, I assume the only meeting you can be talking about is the one where you deliver this letter, where you say that Mr. Milosevic was very upset and yelling and make a lot of noise and -- my apologies. And the witness answered in respect to a representation made by counsel: "Well, there were several meetings," and the witness is answering in the context without re -- I would probably have to read the entire page, but the context -- if I may represent to the Court, the context of when this meeting in which Mr. Milutinovic just fell into place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's a reference to Milosevic. It's not a reference to Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question started out as to when is it this meeting that he says took place on the 25th that he says -- 24th, that he says Mr. Milutinovic participated in on the 24th took place, because it was discovered that his diary indicated that he was at dinner in Pristina on the 24th. So the witness is speaking about the meetings -- the meeting that he thought was on the 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's never been any suggestion so far in the evidence that Mr. Milutinovic met the witness twice, has there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe what the witness is saying here at the passage is I just cited from 11842 forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where he speaks explicitly on the 24th of a meeting with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In cross -- and Mr. Milutinovic. In cross-examination he's referred back to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he says: "I am not sure about the date of the meeting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There were more than one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The meeting that we're discussing on the 24th is a meeting in which he was asked explicitly who were there and he says Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic on one side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, give me the page for the reference to more than one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me the page reference, please. Never mind the debate among yourselves. Just give me the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no reference to more than one a meeting at 11861.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 1194 -- as I indicated, one has to look at the progression of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But it's in the context of meeting Milosevic he says there were several meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness was asked about the meeting with Mr. Milutinovic that took place on the 24th. He was cross-examined about this. That's the second passage that I cited. So he's speaking in the context of a meeting which he thought occurred on the 24th with Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Milosevic, and others. The cross-examination later on focused on the same meeting and the witness is saying, Well, I'm not sure about the date or dates, there were several meetings. Now, the witness does not in any of -- apart from when I examined him directly, explicitly name everybody in these meetings that he's speaking about, but the cross-examination proceeded on the basis of the examination-in-chief about this meeting on the 24th when these named persons were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the second reference you gave me, the first part of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it 861?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 861, Your Honour. 11861.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, I can't see the edge of my transcript, but the answer was: "I can tell you it's a possibility that he was not there," is it? The word's off the end of my -- it's 11862, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "It's been eight years like you said, my notes are what my ..." What's the next word?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "My notes are what my notes say and I relied on my notes at the time."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is this referred to in his notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- the meetings with Mr. Milosevic are not referred to in his notes because those notebooks are unavailable; they are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What transpired -- that is why one has to look at the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination of my friend, and the way it progressed. In chief he gave answers in respect to the 24th. When he was cross-examined by my friend he was focused on that date, the 24th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got the point, Mr. Stamp. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we'll allow you to seek to clarify this with exclusively open questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can now proceed, Mr. Phillips. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us in examination-in-chief that you were present at a meeting with Mr. Milosevic on the 24th of November and you also said in cross-examination that Mr. -- I withdraw that and I start again. You told us in examination-in-chief that you were present at a meeting with Mr. Milosevic, where Mr. Milutinovic was also present, on the 24th of November. And you also said in cross-examination that Mr. Milutinovic might not have been there. Can you explain those two statements, please.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having thought about this last night, I was at a meeting with Mr. Milosevic where I am certain at one of the meetings Mr. Milutinovic was present. I may have mixed up my dates on the 24th. There is some confusion, because we had a state dinner at the Intercontinental Hotel with many of those same players. It is possible it was 4 December when that meeting had taken place, but I am confused on the date and I am fairly certain that at the first or second meeting with Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Milutinovic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at the meeting that Mr. Milutinovic was present at, what were the matters discussed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this meeting was a letter that was submitted to Mr. Milosevic that was outlining areas of noncompliance by Serbian security forces, and we were delivering a note to Mr. Milosevic to that effect -- or a letter to Mr. Milosevic to that effect. And I can't recall at this point if -- I know Mr. Walker wrote it but I can't recall if Ambassador Miles actually handed it to Mr. Milosevic or if Mr. Walker did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were in chief I showed you a letter which was basically setting out the framework of the KVM mission that you said was delivered to Mr. Milosevic. Was this the same letter that you now speak of or was it a different letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a different letter. This OSCE letter outlining the framework I believe was the first letter that was a relatively friendly meeting with Mr. Milosevic that was a courtesy by Mr. Walker to Mr. Milosevic to show him that we were there, that we were on the ground, and this was the parameters of our mission mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall if at that meeting at which Mr. Milutinovic was present if he said anything?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not speak, although at one point Mr. Milosevic conferred with him on a matter but it was nothing that I heard or understood, but spoke very little, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did we not at some stage see a letter drafted on the 23rd of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 24th of November, and if I may -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 23rd, I think, Mr. Stamp. And was that not a letter about noncomplying or was this a friendly letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The exhibit P396 which I showed him - and Your Honour's indeed correct - it's dated the 23rd of November I think is what caused the confusion, the responsibility being entirely mine. I sought to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's that letter about, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This letter is a letter setting out the framework of the operations of the KVM mission dealing with the issues as to the definition of heavy weapons, check-points, observation points, and this is what I showed the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- please carry on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may. My recollection of the sequence was he was -- the witness was shown the letter. He said, Yes, that's the letter we took to Milosevic on the 24th and when he saw it, it got him very upset. So I don't think it's Mr. Stamp's fault. I think the witness saw this letter, confirmed this was the letter that was shown to Milosevic on the 24th and the one that got him upset. And the testimony today is now different for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't think this is the time and place for a submission, but I should place on the record that that is not a correct argument. But if -- but when the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're right, it's a matter for later. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were questioned about your meetings with Mr. Lukic and the absence of a record -- of many records of those meetings in your notes that you took at the time. And you indicated that sometimes you did not accurately record all the persons present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like -- and I think I need to ask leave of the Court, I'd like leave to seek to put to the witness a part of his notes or a part of the notes of his interview in 2001 to see if that could refresh his memory. Before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking, and I think you've already said that, to members of the OTP in 2001?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall discussing at that time meetings that you might have had with Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met with Mr. Lukic in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall discussing with people from the OTP --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milbert Shin who is OTP asked me some questions regarding those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you answered to the best of your recollection then?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I indicated to you what your answers were, would that help you to recall what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly willing to try.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like to seek to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Very well. I take it we should go back to closed session for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I take it the approach you're now taking is a concession that these notes are actually a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a very involved legal discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No if you're putting something to the witness that he's supposed to have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you wouldn't normally be allowed to put something to a witness something that someone else wrote down that he thought he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The notes contain a record of what he said and also other material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's interesting support for the Trial Chamber's view. Please continue. 5 [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in closed session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
