utterances.text: You said or it is recorded here that you said that in respect to a meeting that you had with Serb government officials - and this is page 5 of those notes - "On another occasion prior to Racak but after 15th December 1998, Phillips recalls that Walker asked Sainovic if he could remove the MUP from some other location. Phillips could not recall. Sainovic turned to Lukic and indicated he should deal with the situation. Phillips recalls that the MUP were indeed pulled out. Phillips also recalls" -- okay stop there. Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you answer that. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, the Prosecutor informed us that he would not be using those notes; now he's using them. And on top of it, using them against Sainovic which he had not notified. This is a very unusual trial. I've never seen any such thing in my life before. If he had notified us that he would not be using them he shouldn't be using them. Now in his re-direct he's introducing a new category, and in this new category there is an attack against Sainovic. I move that all this be struck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that the question is beyond the scope of either the direct or the cross that has occurred to date. If indeed he's going to go through all the allegations that are written down by his investigator in these notes, then unfortunately my cross-examination is not complete because obviously since this was not introduced into evidence I did not address these many points and I indeed shortened my cross-examination by about half. If he's going to go into these areas then I'm going to reserve the right to re-cross, but I think it's improper given that this is not a statement and he had ample opportunity to explore these areas in his direct examination, which he did not do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I agree with my friend Mr. Fila that it does not arise in respect to Mr. Sainovic, and the purport of the re-examination on this score is not in respect to Mr. Sainovic. But Mr. Lukic -- cross-examination for Mr. Lukic did refer to this statement and it did refer to this -- not -- I'm so sorry. It did refer to these interview notes, and specifically for the purpose of trying to establish that there were few meetings with Mr. Lukic. These notes were used by counsel as well as the notes -- the contemporaneous notes, in an attempt to establish that there were few or perhaps one meeting with Mr. Lukic. So what I want to ask him is having heard that, that's a record of what he said, can he recall that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This does not arise out of cross-examination, so we will refuse to allow that question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well thank you very much, Your Honour. Then that is the re-examination. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stamp suggested that I had misled you with my last intervention, which he described as a submission --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I never did that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had enough on that, Mr. Ackerman. We'll hear submissions when the time comes. He didn't accuse you of misleading us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think he said I was wrong, but I'll give up on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- that's hardly an accusation of misleading us. I'm sure that there will be hundreds of occasions when he'll allege you wrong between now and the end of this trial. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you want to take anything up? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I would not want to be interrupted before the break by the break. I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm happy to break now if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you would prefer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same routine as yesterday, Mr. Phillips, about half an hour, quarter past 11.00, we'll be back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could go with the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, do we need the closed session for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, we don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Further cross-examination by Mr. O'Sullivan:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday during your examination-in-chief when the Prosecutor was asking you questions, he showed you the letter of 23 November 1998, which is Exhibit P396; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the OSCE --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. Now, a few minutes ago before the break - I'm looking at the transcript now - the Prosecutor asked you this question. He said: "When you were in chief," examination-in-chief, "I showed you a letter which was basically setting out the framework of the KVM mission that you said was delivered to Mr. Milosevic," that's the letter we're talking about, 23rd of November. Then he asked you this question: "Was this the same letter you now speak of or was it a different letter?" And you answered: "I believe it was a different letter. This OSCE letter outlining the framework I believe was the first letter that was a relatively friendly meeting with Mr. Milosevic that was a courtesy by Mr. Walker to Mr. Milosevic to show him that we were there, that we were on the ground, and this was the parameters of our mission mandate." Then there's the question: "Can you recall at that meeting in which Mr. Milutinovic was present if he said anything?" And you answered: "He did not speak, although at one point Mr. Milosevic conferred with him on a matter but it was nothing that I heard or understood but spoke very little of, if at all." So you are saying that there is a letter that this first letter obviously preceded the 23 November 1998 letter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I am struggling with two dates and two letters and the timing of both. To the best of my recollection the OSCE parameter letter was first, there was another letter that was second that was of a compliance nature, which is the one that bothered Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And when you say "the first letter" --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the OSCE letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. Which would be before the 23rd of November, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. Now, I can represent to you that Mr. Walker met with Mr. Milosevic on the 16th of November..

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up Exhibit 1D476, and I'd like the usher to hand the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just wait until the document appears on the screen. I'm giving you a hard copy for you to follow. Sir, do you read Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Turn to the second page of that first of that document you have in your hand, could you look at the second page. That's -- what you see there is the front page of the newspaper called Politika, it's a Belgrade daily, and it's dated the 17th of November, 1998, and the first page, if you go back to it, I just want to show you what it is -- it is a translation of certain passages from that front page which are relevant to my questions for you. And if you had a chance to look quickly at that --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see that it sayings that Ambassador Walker and his associates met with President Milosevic yesterday, and you can see they were talking about the mission. And you'll note that the only other person present at that meeting is Mr. Sainovic, who, as we know, is the head of the cooperation commission with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, sir, my point yesterday and my point today is that you are mistaken, your memory has failed you, and Mr. Milutinovic was never a participant in a meeting where you were present with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, the best I can tell you is I can't -- I can't dispute that. I am struggling with the memory of eight years ago on this. My notes are what my notes are and I rely on them after this period of time and I very well could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I see P396 on the screen, please. Can we just move it up. Thanks. That's okay. Just leave it. And the last -- next page, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does looking at that letter help you at all saying whether that one was presented in the context of a friendly meeting or a meeting at which there was anger expressed?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- there was one meeting that was -- that was friendly. Mr. Milosevic came out, shook Ambassador Walker's hand in a vigorous manner. There was another meeting and there was a letter that went with that meeting about noncompliance issues, and it was not as friendly a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can we take it that this is not the letter about noncompliance meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About noncompliance, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything arising out of that question that's just been asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, that completes your evidence -- oh, sorry. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Your Honour. Yesterday Your Honour, and I think also Mr. Stamp, invited me to let the provider know if there were matters post-Rambouillet that we wanted to raise and I've done that, and I'm still waiting to hear Mr. Stamp's final resolution of this or comment on this. This was done in e-mail last night, e-mail this morning, and in conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We did invite counsel if they wanted to ask anything outside of the notebooks and the scope of the examination-in-chief to let us know yesterday or last night so we could clear it transatlantically -- we got this today and we are in the situation of having to do the same thing, clearing it on the spot, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, the e-mail was sent last night, when you say you got it today. I sent an e-mail last night about this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the bottom line is that he can ask about these matters. We don't object to him asking about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Stamp. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's involved in this, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Very brief. I'd say it's going to take about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just one issue. Is that what you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It's one issue and it refers to the post-Rambouillet. This is on the alleged excessive force and alleged KLA -- excessive KLA reactions to that alleged excessive force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Same -- and, Your Honour, we had a number of exhibits that I mentioned yesterday for the record that we were going to go into, but several of those -- most of those have been already referred to in prior testimony. There are only two matters that I want to inquire, and this will be very brief. Further cross-examination by Mr. Sepenuk:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And again, Good morning, Colonel Phillips. The first item I wanted to ask you about concerned post-Rambouillet, you don't have notes covering that, and this is a period in early March of 1999 and we have the notebooks of General DZ. He also kept notes of what he was doing, he kept diaries of what he was doing. And in his diary for the period March 1st, 1999, he says this about KLA actions. "KLA actions on the ground are becoming increasingly unrestrained. The return of the KLA leadership from France on 25 February does not appear to have affected the situation for the good. KLA have taken hostages in the Prizren region in the latest incident in a space of detentions by the KLA. There has also been KLA activity around Kacanik, an area which has been very quiet in recent months." And my question to you, Colonel, is: Do you -- does your memory jive -- is your memory in accord with what General DZ said in his diaries?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. And then the last question I have for you -- actually, there's another matter that General DZ put in his diaries on March 2nd, 1999, he's talking about hostages and he says: "The two Serb wood-cutters who had been taken hostage were handed over by the KLA in less than mint condition. One was dead, the other had been badly beaten. The handover only happened because of KVM's persistence with the KLA and there had been a number of high-level appeals to the KLA up to and including HOM." Does that also purport with your --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And then the last question I have concerns a KVM fusion centre report of -- and it's an OTP Exhibit 407 number 03525397, and this report talks about an ambush in Pristina at approximately 1815 hours on 21 March 1999: "Four MUP were shot and killed and one was wounded in an ambush. The attack happened near the Hotel Dea, D-e-a, in Pristina. The area has been sealed off and a MUP investigation in ongoing." And the comment is: "This attack appears to have been carried out by the KLA, the first urban KLA attack against the MUP in Pristina. This could become a flashpoint for Serb retaliation against Pristina residents." Do you recall that event of March 21, 1999, the ambush by the KLA of MUP personnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the ambush and some extensive discussion on this, just the urban nature of the KLA not just in Pristina but in other villages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In other words, the attacks were starting to include urban areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Your Honour, there's one point for the transcript, page 56, line 2, I believe the first word should be spaked not spaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, for taking your time but I expected you to ask that question because it doesn't arise out of cross-examination so I could not raise it myself. The witness said yesterday that the Milosevic-Holbrooke agreement was something that Milosevic didn't want to sign. I could not explore more as Defence, but all of us here are interested in whether this agreement exists in writing. And I would appreciate it very much if you could ask the witness whether he knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to me asking that question, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, not if you ask it. Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are fairly glib references made from time to time to a number of agreements which are named after the so-called participants in these agreements, and one of them is the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. Do you know if it exists in written form?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it does, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have. This was initially the agreement that actually allowed OSCE to stand itself up. I do not believe -- when I looked at it I believe it was the foreign minister who had actually signed that document and not Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think further exploration of this is not likely to be fruitful. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to assist you if you allow me. The witness is obviously referring to the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, that's -- I think that it is unlikely to assist us to try to explore recollection now of something that we don't have a copy of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just one small matter with the transcript, it's 56, 22, it says "the Aleksander." Actually it is the attack happened. It says the Aleksander happened near the Hotel Dea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And do you have any re-examination on the point that was raised by Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That now completes your evidence, Mr. Phillips. We are very grateful to you to coming here to give evidence to the Tribunal. I think it only right also to record the Trial Chamber's gratitude to Ms. Manning and Mr. Horrigan for their assistance here and also for the very cooperative way in which yesterday they assisted the expediency of the conclusion of this trial by very quickly taking instructions on matters which required urgent consideration. So thank you again, Mr. Phillips. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I asked you yesterday about one of the exhibits in your second request for admission from the bar table, and my concern was related to the exact nature of a piece taken from the internet. Have you been able to advance investigation into that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No advance, Your Honour. I'll tell you what I have done and what I know. It appears that that interview was done in connection with a documentary that was presented on PBS, the Public Broadcasting System, on a programme called Frontline. I don't know from what I've been able to discover so far whether or not the general -- General Pavkovic's interview was a part of the -- of the portion that was ultimately selected for broadcast. I've only been able to locate two segments, and his was not in those two segments that were broadcast. We are trying to make connections with officials there to see if we can find the original interview tapes in the Serbian language but we don't have it and I don't have any information that his interview was actually broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. There's a general point arising from this because a number of the exhibits that you seek to tender through Mr. Coo are documents which are available only in English but plainly in their original form were either broadcast or printed in Serbo-Croat. Now, what's your submission about how we could satisfy ourselves about the authenticity of the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think sitting in your seat, I would want to see the original Serbian from which the English was transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think it's satisfactory for you to have our Serbian translation of our English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So there is a problem that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how it's to be addressed is not yet clear. We'll turn to that in a moment. I want to do two things at this stage. I want to deal with the request for the admission of exhibits from the bar table, that's the second one filed on the 9th of March. We grant the application to exceed the word limitation. We considered the application along with responses from the accused Sainovic and Pavkovic. The accused Milutinovic joined the Pavkovic response. The Chamber recognises that its requirement that the Prosecution should explain the relevance of each document to issues in the trial has led to the inclusion of argument about the interpretation of the exhibits in the submissions. The Chamber has confined its consideration to the question whether each exhibit should be admitted and has made that determination on the basis of the apparent authenticity and reliability and the prima facie irrelevance of each exhibit. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit all the exhibits tendered in this motion with the exception of the one which we have just been discussing, which is P1378. It's obviously open to the Prosecution to re-tender that with appropriate supporting material. We have decided to exhibit -- to admit all the others because we are satisfied that there are sufficient indicia of authenticity and reliability and a sufficient indication of relevance to do so. We wish to add something about those where objection was taken to their admission. In its final deliberations, the Chamber will give careful consideration to the interpretation of these documents in light of all evidence bearing upon them. P531 and 1947 raised objections which were essentially challenges to the Prosecution's interpretation of the documents rather than their admissibility, and the same was the case in relation to 973 and 969. And there will be a number of others on which I will make the same comment. Exhibit 1010 appears to be a published verbatim account of a statement made by the accused Ojdanic. The Chamber, as has been indicated before, will consider admitting media reports of verbatim statements by the accused where it's satisfied that the report is reasonably capable of challenge by the accused and that its probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. And this particular one falls into that category. In relation to Exhibit 1012, again we regard the submission as essentially about the appropriate interpretation. We take together Exhibits 1063 and 1064. These a Joint Command documents in 1998. The Trial Chamber considers they are relevant to issues in the trial and that the further arguments advanced on behalf of -- well, particularly by Mr. -- on behalf of the accused Sainovic relate essentially to the interpretation of these documents. 1157 and 1160 are again documents where the objection relates principally to their interpretation and they do, in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, bear to be genuine. In relation to 1198, much of the objection there challenges the Prosecution's interpretation of the document, and the other challenges do not indicate that it is other than admissible. Objection was taken by all three accused who objected to a series of exhibits between 799 and 803. The first of these was I think - and I'm pretty sure - mistakenly identified as 779 in Mr. Fila's submission. We've assumed it was 799. Again, that objection essentially challenges the Prosecution interpretation of the documents and, as we have said, that's a matter for later. I turn now to 1101. We consider that is relevant to a period covered by the indictment, and beyond that the objection is again related to interpretation. 1401, the objection relates essentially to interpretation. 1428 is objected to in part because the proposed corroborative document or the one it is said to corroborate, is not in evidence, and that is P1468. Well, again the objection to 1428 is essentially an objection to -- or an argument about its interpretation. But having reflected on the relationship between these two documents and having looked again at P1468, which is the handwritten document entitled: "Meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" detailing 69 separate meetings in 1998, the Chamber has decided to reconsider the decision it made on the 15th of December not to admit the exhibit. Having done that, we consider that what's said in paragraphs 13 to 15 of the Prosecution motion of the 29th of January in combination with the relationship between this document and 1428 leads to the conclusion that it is necessary to admit the document in order to prevent injustice to the Prosecution. On closely examining 1468, the Trial Chamber is now satisfied that it bears the appearance of being an authentic rather than a forged document. There is then objection taken to a series of documents between 1429 and 1435. I take 1429, 1434, and 1440 together. These are each relevant to an anti-terrorist operation in 1998 and thus to paragraph 95 of the indictment. 1433 is a 1998 document which is plainly relevant to issues in the trial. 1432 and 1435 relate to events in 1998 which the Trial Chamber consider to be relevant issues in the trial. Much of the objection taken to these related to the Prosecution's interpretation. 1523 is an Article in Glas Javnosti dated the 18th of July, 1999 reporting the transcript of a TV Top Show appearance of the accused Pavkovic and Lazarevic on Nis television, channel 5, on 16th July 1999. It is in the original language and appears to be a verbatim record of what was said and for these reasons we consider it should be admitted. 1528 is from the same publication, but on the 30th of January, 2001, and is a report of the appointment of the accused Lukic as the new chief of the MUP -- sorry, as the new chief of the RJB of the MUP and of Radosavljevic as the chief of the PJP. The report is in very specific terms and its accuracy can, if appropriate, be challenged. We consider it appropriate to admit that document, albeit it is a press report. 1855, although that document relates to 1990, that is a period on which the Trial Chamber has heard some political and historical background evidence. This document goes no further than that and indeed has an element of formality that may be helpful to us in reaching such few conclusions as may be necessary in relation to that period. So that deals with the request. I now wish to deal with the filing of the 19th of March which is the further submission to joint Prosecution and Defence submission of Annex C, that's documents agreed by the parties, filed on the 9th of March. This filing now includes the exhibit numbers and makes it clear that all but two contained in the original document are agreed. We have also identified two which have already been admitted. The two to which -- on which there is plainly no agreement are 885 and 904. The two already admitted are 1348 and 1635. The remainder of the document in this filing, having been agreed to and assigned an exhibit number, are hereby admitted into evidence. I have one question for Mr. O'Sullivan arising out of this. What's the position of the Weller book? Is it one of these documents or --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Weller book is not one of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you extracted things from it and agreed them in this one? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is to be its position?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The book -- and the pages from the book that were used in evidence are recorded in the e-court system, so it's Exhibit 1D18 with a page range, which represents the actual documents that were used with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have you sought agreement of the Prosecution that these are an accurate reflection of events?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, we haven't, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would it not be a good idea? Because it seems a handy way of reviewing the events of Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, were you about to leave that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to indicate to you that there are a number of other documents on there that were previously admitted into evidence, Prosecution exhibits were previously admitted through your October order, but I don't know if those have all been identified. I don't have the list in front of me, but a number of them were admitted but the Defence had agreed they wanted to leave them on the list and I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Hannis, that what the agreement does is advance the situation to the point where parties are all agreed that these documents are what they bear to be, whereas previously you were tendering documents that the Defence were still indicating that they might challenge. So I think there's no harm done by clarifying that through this agreement. That takes us to the question of the proposed written statement to be introduced in the evidence of Philip Coo. Just a couple of introductory comments before we hear any further submissions on this. A number of detailed objections to parts of the proposed statement have been made on the basis that they bear to be conclusions, which is not appropriate for this witness to make. Our broad impression of the document in its current form is that most of the objectionable conclusions of that nature have been removed and that, although there are statements which might be capable of being described as conclusions, they are in many instances plainly open to the clear interpretation that they are just a statement of fact or a statement almost of the obvious from what's in the document. And we do think you should be able to trust us to distinguish between the two. You can take it we will at no point accept a conclusion that Mr. Coo has drawn that would be appropriate only for an expert or the Court itself to draw. Now, in making that observation I'm trying to simplify this to some extent, because otherwise this can be a very lengthy exercise. The second general comment I would wish to make is that a large number of the exhibits suffer from the same difficulty as the one in the order we've just dealt with. They originally existed in Serbo-Croat and have been translated, but the original version -- translated into English, but the original version is no longer available. And while we will have to make a final decision on this, you've heard the Prosecution position on the one we discussed earlier and I assume it will be the same in relation to all the others. So that is a broad category, again, of material which might affect some of the passages, apart from the exhibit itself, the passages in the proposed statement. And the final preliminary point I wish to make is this. Objection is taken to the first part of the report setting out the legislative structure. We have to consider further whether this is something that should not be admitted. It's actually very helpful to see the material related in the way in which it has been related. We can see the link between provisions, rules, regulations, and statutes. On the other hand, we can also read the law for ourselves and the Prosecution can make submissions about the law and the effect of the regulations. So we see two arguments that can plainly be advanced here. We wouldn't like to lose assistance in the end of the day, as long as it's kept within bounds. We will probably, if we do decide that large parts of this have to be removed for reasons such as that, then we may feel obliged to instruct a military expert ourselves, depending on the assistance that we can find in the material without that. We'd obviously like to avoid having to do it, but that might be an alternative. Now, bearing in mind that something of that nature may be necessary to assist us, we invite you to be restrained in your submissions about the impact of the report, set out the way it is now. We recognise that opinion and conclusion are inappropriate; on the other hand, we would appreciate the assistance that can be derived from someone putting the material into reasonable order. If there are significant additional submissions to be made by Defence counsel on top of what's been submitted in writing, then it would be appropriate for us to hear these first before inviting Mr. Hannis to respond. If, on the other hand, all that's sought by the request for oral argument is to supplement what's here already, then it may be it's unnecessary. That's a matter for Defence counsel to judge. Mr. Ackerman, you, I think, were leading the van on this. Do you want to say anything further at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I put a sentence at the end of the submission that I would like an opportunity for additional oral submission, and that was just in case something came up in the meantime that I hadn't had a chance to deal with. I think it would be excessive for me to go further in view of the motion I filed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Fila, you are the other main player here. Do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I merely wanted to say that we received the materials in B/C/S only yesterday afternoon, and I think that in fact we did need some more time to consult with our clients. We're talking about a thousand pages or more, but we -- I did agree with Mr. Hannis that Mr. Coo might start tomorrow and then we will make up for it. We will catch up. What I wanted to say that the persistence in tendering this statement reminded me of something that Marcus Tullius Cicero said in the senate. Let me quote something in Latin when he spoke about Catalina, a Roman nobleman "quo usque tandem abutere, o Catalina, patientia nostra." And I don't think that we need the fifth booth. I think this actually is an apt comment to make regarding Mr. Coo and I will stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was one question for Mr. Ackerman I forgot to ask. Is the list at the end simply a summary of what's in the main part of your document or does it add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think there are some exhibits listed there that I don't talk about in the main part of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is find the exhibit time for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's just to make -- actually I didn't prepare that myself, Your Honour, I commissioned it. And I think there are some documents listed there that are not in the body. I just wanted to make sure that there was a record of my objections to the exhibits that are, in my view, objectionable. So there may be some there that are not in the body of the thing. Probably are. And I think there are two there that are mistakes and we debated whether to file a corrigendum or not. And if the Chamber wishes me to identify those, I can't do it immediately but I can probably do it rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you did two things, identified mistakes and identified those in that list at the end that are not dealt with substantially in the report -- in the submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't do it now, but I can do it before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No -- yeah, that would be helpful. There was a fourth comment I should have made as a preliminary. The reference in paragraph 14 of your submission, Mr. Ackerman, to the executive summary and the other introductory summaries we do agree with that submission. We think that there's neither need for it nor a sound basis for it. It doesn't really greatly affect the issue but that was easily dealt with. And if I may now ask you a few questions just to clarify things that we've identified, if you don't mind assisting us further. The -- do you really think that he comments greatly on laws, regulations, and decrees, rather than simply relating them one to the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that -- I think that comment is in the submission based upon the order that you announced orally I think on the 9th of March, where you said he had no place commenting on such matters. And in our view, the report was not changed in any significant way from how it had existed at that point in time. So the assumption was made that you had basically already made the determination that that was improper and it was just set out in there in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it's fair to the report to say that it's not been substantially altered in that part. If you just flick -- in fact, I know you have got the one which has got the blacked-out portions and there are a fair number of them. And having said that, we are -- obviously we don't want to make decisions that are inconsistent and if we feel that he's doing more than simply identifying the laws that comment on things that a military analyst might be familiar with, that is the structure of military units and the powers that they have to exercise and so on and simply identifying them, if we think he's going further than that then obviously we will pay no attention to it. But actually identifying the ones which do refer to things such as, for example, discipline and whatever. I wonder if there's anything wrong with that and if we went too far if we suggested that he should never refer to the law at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, frankly I see no problem with him identifying various documents as being relevant to issues that might be important in the case. If he starts going -- taking the next step and defining what he believes that relevance is and the findings that you should make in that regard, then I think that becomes the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, immediately following what we've just been looking at in paragraph 16 there's an example of that -- that's paragraph 16 of your submission. But having said that, you can take it we would never be misled by a comment like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and that underscores the point that I think -- I think it was something more than just a statement of the existence of these laws, but some conclusions drawn from them. And what Your Honour has said this morning, if this report is going to be taken in the light that you've suggested, that is, if there are any conclusions in it they'll be ignored, then how could I not trust the Chamber to do that? I mean that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, at least you couldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I have a number of other questions, if you don't mind. What is wrong with the Prosecution referring to the VJ web site? I take the point there's a difference between the VJ in general and the individual accused that are before us, but what's wrong with an apparently official web site being a source of material?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no idea and the Prosecution has no idea the parameters under which information is put into that web site, who it is that's authorised to put information into that web site, whether or not there's any effort made to make that information accurate and reliable. You know, it may be somebody that has computer skills but very little knowledge of the VJ that's just kind of putting stuff in there at whim. In other words, there's no basis for us to believe that the material put in that web site is accurate material, and if you want to spend some time surfing around on the net you'll find something in a web site supporting almost any proposition you want to come up with and some of them may be "official" web sites. So I think without some kind of evidence that the material put in that web site was checked and authorised by someone of -- with the ability to do so, I think it's very difficult to say -- just drag something off a web site and say, This proves something. I just don't think that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about simply establishing that it is the official web site of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think that gets there. I think official web sites are subject to error and mistake as any other web site because eventually it comes to some technician sitting in front of a type-writer and typing stuff in and he may type it correctly and he may not and if that technician comes here and says that was information given to me by commanding general of the VJ and it came from an official source and I simply copied it into the web site, then that's no problem but to just assume that that's reliable material because it comes from a web site I think is an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a number of publications attributed to an organisation called Vojska which seems to have something to do with the VJ also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Vojska, Your Honour, is that VJ magazine, the translations of which are not CLSS translations. They apparently come from some US government organisation, and I'm not going to quote a web site --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But are most -- yeah, are most of them items where we don't have the B/C/S original?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no B/C/S original cited. It's not on the web site -- I mean on the e-court. If you go to e-court all you get is the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's the American translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the American translations and I think they were done by an organ of the CIA primarily, which at least recent history should teach us not to completely trust.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On a number of occasions you refer to something as a report and then say that for that reason it's inadmissible. It's not clear to me why you say that. Reports compiled in the course of official duty would normally be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. Do you have a paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I need to find one of them. If you take paragraph 20, and when I had a look at this it's actually a 3rd Army order I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not able to respond, Your Honour, because 20 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've clarified to some extent by saying that you commissioned this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Much of this I did myself. I think paragraph 20 I probably did myself, but in terms of trying to connect that to something without the Coo books here in front of me, I'm not able to do that right now. I'd have to be able to look at footnote 39 and I don't have it here. But there must have been something about that that distressed me because I think there are other reports that I have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's another one that -- another example is 25, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think this probably arises, Your Honour, from language in your March 9th oral order, and I also haven't got that in my hand, but I think it arises from some language there that it was inappropriate for him to comment on certain kinds of reports. The difference probably is between reference to a report and comment upon its meaning, and I think that's probably what Your Honours meant on the 9th of March, and that gets us back to your earlier remarks today that, to the extent there were any comments, they would be ignored by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a particularly good example of what might be concerning you if you go to your paragraph 47. Now, I can understand your anxiety about what's said there, but I also find it very difficult to imagine circumstances in which the Trial Chamber would be misled in any way by that. We would look at the whole context and draw our own conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a number of examples, both in the Coo document and I was working through the third bar table submission by the Prosecution last night. There's a tendency by the Prosecution to take a document which makes a request for something and treat it as if that request was honoured exactly as it was made and that it's a fait accompli and that you should then take it that that happened. That's pervasive in many of the Coo comments and Prosecution comments with regard to some of these documents, that a mere request becomes a fact, not beyond the request that it was honoured and acted upon. And I don't think that's appropriate. And again, I think Your Honours are totally capable of seeing and recognising that and ignoring it. Your Honour pointed out this morning that to some extent this process has denigrated to the making of submissions, and I think there's a grain of truth in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't be faulted, though, for trying and that was not meant to be a criticism. It was an acceptance that we, to some extent, had prompted that situation. The problem -- the principal problem in the end of the day is that Mr. Coo could be in the witness box for a few days on end identifying documents that had been recovered by an RFA or had been found here, there, or everywhere, in other words, speaking to the provenance report; whereas a great deal of time could be saved by accepting the basic parts of his report as introducing the documents to their relevant place, as it were, in the case and confirming the accuracy, if he can, of the provenance document itself. So there are choices here to be made about what is necessary to satisfy us about the authenticity of this material, quite apart from the question of whether Mr. Coo goes too far. Whatever we decide here, the Prosecution are clearly going to seek to introduce a substantial number of documents through Mr. Coo one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that regard I hear what you're saying and I have a suggestion which I think solves everyone's problem perhaps, and that is this: It's based upon our argument in this motion that what you have before you is basically a submission by the Prosecution through Mr. Coo. And I'm perfectly willing to have the Trial Chamber treat that as a submission by Mr. Hannis of his fourth bar table request. And if you treat it as a fourth bar table request, then it becomes a submission by the Prosecution that is not evidence in the case. When it becomes evidence in the case, it takes on a completely different light than when it's a submission that, Here is a bunch of documents that ought to be admitted. And if you want to treat it as a bar table submission, you've already got my response to whether or not I believe those documents are admissible or not and you make the determination today what's admissible and what's not and we know exactly what to do tomorrow with Mr. Coo. And then we don't have to spend hours on cross-examination, going page after page through what is a Coo report as opposed to a submission by the Prosecution which we wouldn't be cross-examining on. That may be the solution to the problem you just talked about, because otherwise what Mr. Visnjic said yesterday was not said in jest. There is a -- either a five-minute or a five-hour cross-examination of Coo depending on what it is we're dealing with. If we're dealing with all of these pages of material as a Coo report document, then that requires cross-examination that wouldn't happen if it were treated as simply a submission and a request for the admission of documents. If we treat it that way, then I don't think we have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where would you like me to begin, Your Honour? I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, begin at the end. That might be a good idea. You've been offered a -- or a suggestion has been made by Mr. Ackerman about how this could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I came to court today I was working on two tracks and one was trying to file a -- draft a written response to Mr. Ackerman's most recent submission, but you've addressed a number of those issues already so I don't think I have to. Your first point about conclusions, I think we have removed the most objectionable of those. Any that remain are ones that Your Honours will be able to draw on your own or ignore them if you disagree. A large number of the exhibits do suffer from the point you raised in connection with Exhibit P1378 and the Vojska materials are an example of that, because we don't have the original B/C/S from the Vojska magazine; in many cases, what we have is the FBIS translation, the English translation. But one thing I would indicate in connection with many of those, if not most of those articles, we're offering them for a limited purpose. A limited purpose many times is just simply to show the identification of a particular individual in connection with the particular unit, perhaps. It's an army magazine, article, and will talk about the heroics of the 549th Motorised Brigade but it will mention Delic as the commander and it might mention that they were in this location on that day. Much of that is corroborated through other evidence and it's only in Coo's report as sort of supplemental information about who was the commander at that time which helps him draw up his chart. But we also have that from other more authentic documents, daily combat reports signed by Delic as the commander of the 549th. So to the extent that we will continue to try to offer it, most of those are for limited purposes. The second track I had been working on was going through the provenance report and the list of documents, and I think it was 438 or something like that. Approximately 60 of those are already admitted exhibits, so those can go out. I'm not trying to get them in through Coo, but they are referred to in his report to relate to other matters and to explain other documents. But in my rough go-through before court today, I think probably half of them are not ones that are must-have exhibits from the Prosecution's point of view. It may be necessary for the continuity and flow of Coo's report, statement, whatever we're calling it now, but they're not ones that I want to tender on their own for you to look at for all purposes, not just for some limited purpose. You made that remark concerning the legislative structure and the constitutional provisions, the Law on Defence, et cetera, and I think you have a right, Your Honour. Mr. Coo is not commenting on those except to the extent that he quotes what's in them and then relates them to other documents or structures that we see. The objection to the summary overview we understand is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you lost that whole part, what would you actually have lost?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to sit back and read it again. I think not a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You could put it in as a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just been invited to do that. You know, we're not in the business of just admitting something because it might not fail a test. We, I think, should be more concerned about admitting things which pass a qualification, and therefore there must be a purpose in presenting the evidence. That large swathe of material about the set-up, the structure, the legislation, the regulations, the rules, all seems to be stuff that has been agreed or will be admitted in some form on which you can then reproduce this document as your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and many of those have already been admitted, either through your first order in October last year or through other witnesses, so much of that is in place. And I am interested in the proposal that we sort of tender Mr. Coo's report as our submission. But I feel like I need to respond to some of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions but I'd rather you made your submissions first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The other remarks, the questions you addressed to Mr. Ackerman. I would point out one thing. With regard to paragraph 47, which Your Honour pointed to as an example where he may have made an overstatement, that's where there was a request for weapons and Coo, in his report, leaves it as though that was granted. Mr. Coo and I looked at that yesterday and Mr. Ackerman is right. Mr. Coo is wrong on that because there's nothing in that document to show that weapons were given. There's other evidence in the case that may suggest that that, indeed, happened but that's not right. But I would disagree with Mr. Ackerman's further submission that that's a pervasive kind of thing in the report and a pervasive kind of thing in our submissions for bar table exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that where it does crop up it can be crossed on anyway, and this would have been a good example of one that could have been dealt with easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my submission. If you have specific questions for me, Your Honour, I'll be happy to try and address them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you heard me say that we would probably exclude the executive summary and other introductory summaries, and I take it you have nothing to say to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only thing I was going to say about that in my written response to Mr. Ackerman's submission regarding that was that they are -- I think they are a fair summary of what follows in each case and they are only offered sort of for readability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So they're not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you don't normally have a witness come into court and say, Well, I'll tell you now what my evidence is going to amount to and that will help you focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I seem to recall some witnesses who introduced every answer in some fashion similar to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. You rely on what you claim are official VJ and MUP web sites, and you've heard submissions made about the unreliability of web sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. We can ask Mr. Coo about that when he's here, but that's what he will say, that these are identified as the official web sites for the VJ and for the MUP. The documents that we proposed in connection with that, if you look at the documents themselves, they're really not about things that are very controversial. In one case I think one of the pages we offer is a reference to the constitutional provisions about the role of the army, which we have from the constitution itself. So to some extent the web sites are corroborated by the constitution because it has that information accurately and which you might argue other things from there may be accurate as well. We have descriptions of some of the various types of units that are in the army, and those are consistent with other evidence in the case. From that you might say, Why do I need it at all? We'd say, It's just some further evidence in corroboration of other evidence in the case. I don't recall that there was anything very controversial. I think on the VJ web site there was one statement or press release citing General Pavkovic for some remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, a press release is, I would have thought, essentially an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if it's posted on the web site, Mr. Ackerman has questions about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that change it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can see an argument both ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt it, but I can picture all sorts of things on web sites that I wouldn't be prepared to rely on. But an official VJ web site with a press release, I think there's a pretty good argument that that's got enough indicia of reliability for us to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I certainly don't want to take the position, Your Honour, that we take everything that's on the VJ web site or any web site as being gospel truth no matter what it is. We think you have to look at other things, look at the content itself, see if it's corroborated by other witnesses or other evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're also influenced to some extent by the question how difficult something might be to challenge, and the official nature of a publication would tend to suggest that there will be ways of inquiring into it and challenging it if the accuracy is not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's a good point, Your Honour. If there were some web site out there purporting to be the official VJ web site and saying things that weren't accurate, I would think that somebody from the VJ would notice at some point in time and bring it to the world's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, if you go to paragraph 30 of Mr. Ackerman's, you'll find that there are a number of media reports and transcripts referred to. And probably in relation to all of them there is a question over language and translation that will need to be addressed. In one of them I can't actually tell, the last one I think, footnote 18, it's a television programme. If you've got it in B/C/S, fine. So there are -- there's actually quite a lot of work in this. It's not an easy task and you've identified over 400 of these exhibits. We can't just take a completely broad brush to this and say, Just throw them at us. We'll take them and analyse them. We've really got to be satisfied that what we're taking satisfies the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and with regard to those, if we don't have the original language, then I think we will -- we won't be asking you to take those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you may have to go over all of the language issues here. Paragraph 36 is possibly the best example of all. There are apparently two English versions of this, which I couldn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 36?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of the submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where he refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's about Perisic and it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, it says "Pesic" but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the circumstances in which he left the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may be that both come to the same, but I wasn't able to work out why there are two different versions. There's one in Mr. Coo's report and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was one that was introduced in Milosevic and I think that was taken from a book. We'll have a look at that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be clear to you now what all the translation problems are. Paragraph 45 suggested that there was no reference in the document to the Skorpions, and I certainly couldn't find it quickly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Within the document itself, Your Honour, I don't believe there is, but there was evidence from the witness Goran Stoparic, who identified himself as a Skorpion and identified the author of that document as being the head of the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you'll see here that Mr. Coo has cited the document as an example showing that the Skorpions were brought in as a reserve element of the MUP's SAJ. Now, the document's much more general than that and doesn't refer to the Skorpions. So I'm afraid it's this sort of thing that creates doubt in the mind about whether, in parts, he goes beyond what we ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see your point with regard to that, Your Honour. There was other evidence connecting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a separate issue, I think, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 60, it says that the documents -- all the documents relied on are inadmissible press reports or information from web sites. Well, at a quick glance, it looks to me as though some may be okay, but we really need to know more, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's also some -- an apparent relationship between what's said in paragraph 78 and what's said in paragraph 36 of these submissions. These are the questions I have. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. How to address some of them which you can't address immediately we'll discuss for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you indicated that you had some filing underway or have you departed from that idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I had not departed from it. I just stopped to come to court. But some of the matters that I was addressing in Mr. Ackerman's submission you've already addressed in terms of conclusions and comments on reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you seem to be able to divide your proposed exhibits into those that were essential and those that were desirable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to readily do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think so. If I could sit with Mr. Coo for a couple of hours, I think we could winnow it down. My rough cut, we had gone from what was 434 to 200 something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that would be a very helpful exercise to undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think so, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think also that the law could readily disappear from this report as well without you losing anything, as long as you're satisfied that every item has been introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll have a look at that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And indeed we would obviously allow a little time later in the week for you to double-check that if you're anxious about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So We will adjourn now until tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I could raise one briefly, very briefly. It's about a framework or a timetable in which the Rule 70 provider in respect to the last witness would indicate what aspect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was remiss of me not to have dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence needs to remain in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I should have suggested to you at the end of the evidence was that no later than a week on Friday you make a decision on the material which can be in the public domain, and a hopefully limited amount that does not require -- that requires to remain in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We thought ten days would be ample for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It should be. May I make another request to the Court. I think that one or maybe two of the counsel for the Defence had put into e-court exhibits which comprise the entirety of the -- of the notebooks but only referred to a page or two. If they could remove it from e-court and put in only that page that they used or wanted to use, that might facilitate the provider in raising any restrictions on it being sealed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a comment on that? Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Not really a comment, Your Honour, but just for the sake of the record - it will take 20 seconds - I neglected to mention that the part of General DZ's notebooks was reading from are 3D414, page 32 and page 38. [Realtime transcript read in error.] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I not right in saying that -- well, it may be two counsel. I understood one had placed a bundle of material from the notebooks into the e-court. Is that you, Mr. Ivetic? Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday to Mr. Stamp - and I can repeat - it is very little but if you have trouble giving up those two sentences, if you think that is detrimental to you, that's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, the thing is that if a batch of documents, hundreds of pages, is in e-court, then whereas we might agree that the part used need not be under seal; we couldn't agree to the whole thing. So it could be -- if the situation could be regularised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you please deal with that directly with counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and only draw it to our attention if it's necessary for us to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Page 87, line 19, it should be page 32 and page 38, not 33 that's mentioned there. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need -- I know we're running out of time. I need a few seconds. Mr. Hannis talked about documents being offered just for a limited purpose and I just want to state that that creates future enormous problems because more than once I've stood in the appellate Chamber here and heard a Prosecutor refer to some part of a document that was admitted for a limited purpose but using it for a different purpose at the appeal. So if it's to be admitted for a limited purpose, everything else should be redacted so that there's no question four years down the road from now that that was admitted for any other reason. Second of all, the problem -- another problem with web sites that I didn't refer to you about was that web sites change rather frequently, and it's very difficult to go back years later and check if something actually came off of a web site because it's probably not there any longer. And finally, Your Honour, the two documents I referred to on my chart at the end of the submission are P1588 and P626. P626 is there -- is not there for a purpose and should be removed. P1588, however, is there for a purpose and it deals with a document that appears to be incomplete. It's just filled with blanks, and it's like it was a document that was prepared but never -- never actually filled in the blanks and sent, unless there's some showing that it was actually issued I think it cannot be admitted. And that's all I have to say and we can break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will resume at 9.00 tomorrow, and before then hopefully we'll have indicated something of the likely ruling in relation to the evidence of Mr. Coo.
